groups.title: Naming a field
groups.blurb: A bare name is letters, digits, `_` and `$`, dotted. `source.ip` is one column. A name is the same name wherever it stands: read, written, or passed. `$` is the record itself, an [object](#objects): `$.source.ip` and `source.ip` are one read. A field whose name holds any other character is written `$["..."]`, so `$["source.ip"]` is a different field: one key with a dot in it.

rows.gloss: the field of that dotted name, or a child of an object

examples.note: one flat column

rows.gloss: a field of the record by its name, for one a bare spelling cannot hold

notes: `$["..."]` takes a string literal and names a field, not a value: `$["x-y"].z` is the one field `x-y.z`, as `a.b` is. `$[k]` with `k` a value reads whichever field `k` names on that row, as any object's `o[k]` does.
On a named field, a fixed string key follows the same path: `geo["city"]` reads `geo.city`. A declared field a record lacks reads as null.

rejected.why: `@` cannot start a bare name. Write `$["@timestamp"]`.

groups.title: Objects
groups.blurb: The record is an object: `$` is the whole record, and each field is one of its keys. An object is written `{"a": 1, "b": 2}`. `o[k]` reads the key that `k` holds on each row.

functions.name: keys
functions.summary: The object's keys, as an array of strings, in the order the record writes them. A field holding null is left out.

functions.name: entries
functions.summary: Each key with its value, as `{key, value}`, in the order of `keys`. Every value must be of one type.

functions.name: fromEntries
functions.summary: An object of an array of `{key, value}`. A later key replaces an earlier one, and a null key is left out.

functions.name: omit
functions.summary: The object without those keys.

groups.title: Comparison and logic
groups.blurb: The operators that answer a question or pick a value rather than compute one. None belongs to a single type: comparison works across numbers, text, instants and spans, and `??` takes a value of any type.

rows.gloss: the left value unless it is null

examples.note: the left is null, so the fallback stands in
a null array value uses the fallback
an empty array is already a value

rows.gloss: ternary; if true, then take the first, otherwise take the second

examples.note: the branches widen to a common type

rejected.why: Text and a number have no common type. Convert first: `"10".parseInt() < 9` is `false`.
There is no truthiness: `||` takes `bool` operands.

notes: Both operands of a comparison must have the same type, except that an `i64` beside an `f64` widens to `f64`. Ordering works on numbers, text, instants and spans. Text orders by Unicode code point, so it is case-sensitive: `"Z" < "a"` is `true`. `bool` and `bytes` take `==` and `!=` only.

Comparisons always return a boolean. Equality is true when both values are null, and false when only one is null. `!=` gives the opposite result. Ordering (`<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`) is false if either value is null; null is not converted to zero.

`!`, `&&` and `||` read null as false and always return a boolean. For example, `!null` is `true`, `true && null` is `false`, and `false || null` is `false`. Non-null operands must be booleans; numbers and strings are not converted to true or false.
`??` tests null and nothing else, so `0` and `""` pass through: `"" ?? "fallback"` is `""`. It binds looser than `&&` and `||`, so `a ?? b && c` is `a ?? (b && c)`.
Every branch must compile. Branches whose types do not meet, such as a `str` and an `i64`, give a `variant`.

A `variant`, a value read from an open object `{...}` or made from one, has a type only per row. `== null`, `!= null`, `isNull` and `??` compile on it, and so does a read by a `str` or `i64` key, as `v.k`, `v[k]` or `v[0]`. A read gives a `variant`, null where the row's value holds nothing; a negative index counts from the end. Any other operator, condition or function argument needs a type first, as in `n: i64 = v`. A ternary whose branches are a `variant` and another type is a `variant`: each row keeps the value of the branch it took.
Null and an empty array are different. A conditional array value that selects null stays null: `== null` is true and `??` uses its fallback. The length of a null array is null; `length([])` is `0`.

groups.title: Conversion
groups.blurb: Reading one type as another. A parse whose text does not convert is null on that row and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception on the record; it never returns an approximation. Blank text is null and throws nothing. Text that reads as an instant is read with [parseTime](#parseTime).

A form it does not know is null and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception.

groups.title: Numbers
groups.blurb: `i64` and `f64`. An `i64` beside an `f64` widens to `f64`. An arithmetic `i64` result never wraps. The bitwise operators take `i64` only and work over all 64 bits.

examples.note: by zero is null, not infinity

rows.gloss: remainder, signed like the left operand

examples.note: the sign comes from the left operand, not the right
a zero divisor is null, as dividing by zero is
right-associative, so `2 ** (3 ** 2)`
`000…0` flipped is `111…1`, all 64 bits set

rows.gloss: shift toward the low end, sign-preserving

notes: An `i64` result that does not fit, from `+`, `-`, `*`, negation, `abs`, `idiv`, `round`, `floor`, `ceil` or `trunc`, is null on that row and throws an `Overflow` exception on the record: `9223372036854775807 * 2` is null, not a wrapped negative.
A value divided by zero with `/`, `%` or `idiv` is null on that row and throws a `DivideByZero` exception on the record. A null divided by zero is null and throws nothing.
An `f64` result that is not finite, such as `1e308 * 10`, throws no exception. JSON has no spelling for it, so the output omits the field.

Bitwise operands are signed and already 64 bits wide, so there is no narrowing step and no unsigned shift. The shift count is taken modulo 64, and bits pushed off the end are gone: `1 << 65` is `2`, and `(1 << 62) << 2` is `0`.

groups.title: Arrays
groups.blurb: An `array<T>` holds elements of the one type `T`. `filter` keeps the elements whose condition is true and `map` computes a value for each element. [length](#length), [slice](#slice), [at](#at), [indexOf](#indexOf) and [includes](#includes) take an array or a string.
notes: `+` joins two arrays of the same element type. It never appends a single element, since `xs + y` would be ambiguous when `y` is itself an array; [push](#push) appends.

rejected.why: `+` joins two arrays; use `push` to append an element.

notes: It compiles in an Eval or Code step. In a route condition, a delivery condition or a capture filter it does not compile.
The arrow takes one parameter. Its body is one expression, or a block whose last expression is the value. An arrow may call local functions and hold another arrow.

groups.title: Dates and times
groups.blurb: A datetime is an instant in UTC, microsecond-resolution, and serializes as ISO 8601. `now()` is read once per record, so every route a record takes sees the same instant. There is no local time zone: a log line's own offset is read when it is parsed and kept nowhere else.

examples.note: `now()` is read once per record, so both of these are the same instant

rejected.why: Two instants have no sum. Subtract them for a span.

notes: [Comparison](#tests) orders instants: `start < end` is true when `start` is earlier.

functions.name: now
functions.summary: The current instant. Captured once per record, so every route a record takes sees the same value.

functions.name: parseTime
functions.summary: Parses text into a datetime. With no format, a run of digits is a compact date when it reads as one (`YYYYMMDD` or `YYYYMMDDHHMMSS`), else a Unix epoch whose unit comes from its magnitude — seconds below 10^11, then milliseconds, microseconds and nanoseconds at each further thousand — and other text is matched against the common shapes — ISO 8601, `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`, `YYYY/MM/DD HH:MM:SS`, syslog's `Mon  D HH:MM:SS`, and Apache's `[D/Mon/YYYY:HH:MM:SS +ZZZZ]`. Give a `strftime` format to pin it, and a reference instant to fix the year a syslog stamp does not carry. A parser's declared `datetime` field is this call: the bare type detects, and `{"type":"datetime","format":...}` pins.

examples.note: ten digits of seconds; the same instant in milliseconds, `904478400000`, reads the same
eight digits that read as a date are that date, not a count of seconds
a zone name outside the set `%z` takes is null, never a guess
give the name the offset it means for this source, then parse
auto-detect reads four digits as seconds; `%Q` says milliseconds and `%s` says seconds
no reference means `now()`, which is where a yearless stamp gets its year
a shape auto-detect does not know; the year comes from `now()`
a December line read five minutes into January is last year's, not next year's
the same call, written as a function

functions.specifierBlurb: `parseTime(value, format)` takes these, and only these. Every other byte of the format must match the text literally, and text left over when the format runs out makes the result null rather than a partial read. Auto-detect tries an ordered list of formats built from the same specifiers, so every rule below holds for `parseTime(value)` too.

specifiers.matches: The year, exactly four digits. There is no two-digit year: every century pivot is wrong for someone.
Month number, `1`-`12`, with or without a leading zero.
Day of month, `1`-`31`, with or without a leading zero. A day past the month's end is null.

examples.note: February has no 30th

specifiers.matches: Day of month with an optional leading space, as in `Aug  3`.
Hour on a 24-hour clock, `0`-`23`. `24` is ISO 8601's end-of-day and is allowed only at a zero minute, second and fraction.

examples.note: the midnight that closes the date

specifiers.matches: Hour on a 12-hour clock, `1`-`12`. Pair it with `%p`.
Second, `0`-`60`, two digits. `60` is a leap second and lands on the following minute.
Fractional seconds. Every digit is read and the first six kept, so a nanosecond stamp is truncated rather than refused; a shorter run is a position, not a count.

A UTC offset — `Z`, `+HH`, `+HHMM` or `+HH:MM` — or one of the named zones `UT`, `UTC`, `GMT`, `EST`, `EDT`, `CST`, `CDT`, `MST`, `MDT`, `PST`, `PDT`. Any other name is null. Without `%z` the text reads as UTC.

examples.note: A whole-hour offset without its minutes

specifiers.matches: An English month name, abbreviated or full. The same specifier as `%B`.
An English month name, abbreviated or full. The same specifier as `%b`.
An English weekday name, abbreviated or full. Consumed and discarded — it is never checked against the date.
An English weekday name, abbreviated or full. The same specifier as `%a`.
`AM` or `PM`, either case. Reads `%I`; `12 AM` is midnight and `12 PM` is noon.
Seconds since the Unix epoch, with an optional sign and fraction. It names the whole instant, so the format holds no other specifier.

examples.note: auto-detect would read a count this small as seconds too; the specifier says so outright

specifiers.matches: Milliseconds since the Unix epoch, with an optional sign and fraction. It names the whole instant, so the format holds no other specifier.

examples.note: auto-detect reads a count this small as seconds

notes: The reference is a datetime, not a year — usually the field carrying when the record was collected. Pass none and it is `now()`, which is what makes the no-argument form right for a live stream.

A yearless stamp takes the reference's year, and rolls back a year rather than landing in the future: parsed against 1 January 1999, `Dec 31` is 1998. That also means an anchor *earlier* than the stamp reads as the year before it.

Text that does not parse is null on that row and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception on the record. An impossible date is such text, never a silently shifted one: `1998-02-30` does not become 2 March.

A zone name is not one offset: `CST` is six hours behind UTC in Chicago and eight ahead in Shanghai, and one pipeline reads both. `%z` takes the fixed set the table names. Replace any other name with the offset that source means — `replaceAll(/CEST/, "+0200")` — and the choice sits beside the source it belongs to.

groups.title: Durations
groups.blurb: A duration is a signed span, microsecond-resolution. Subtracting two datetimes produces one. It serializes as a bare count of microseconds, `toString()` produces the same text, and `parseDuration()` reads it back.
notes: [Comparison](#tests) orders spans: `age > duration(5, "m")` is true when `age` is longer than five minutes.

functions.name: duration
functions.summary: A span of `count` units. The unit is `"ns"`, `"us"`, `"ms"`, `"s"`, `"m"`, `"h"`, `"d"`, `"w"` or a long name, and the count may be fractional.

examples.note: a thousand nanoseconds is one microsecond, exactly
a week is exactly seven days

notes: A span is held to the microsecond, so anything finer truncates toward zero: `duration(1500, "ns")` is one microsecond and `duration(1, "ns")` is a zero span. A fractional count of any unit rounds the same way.
There is no month or year: how long either one is depends on which one, and a span is a count with no calendar attached to answer that. A week is seven days, so it is here.
A literal unit is checked when the pipeline compiles: `duration(1, "y")` does not compile. A unit computed per row that names no unit makes the result null. A span too large to hold is null.

functions.name: countIn
functions.summary: The whole span counted in one unit, as an `f64`, not a remainder.

examples.note: the unit the wire form counts in
the same call, written as a function

rejected.why: A year varies in length, so a span cannot be counted in one. Days are fixed: `duration(365, "d")`.

groups.title: Addresses and networks
groups.blurb: An address is text. A function parses it and writes it back as text. Text that is not an address makes the result null and throws no exception. Space around an address is ignored. To match an address against a table of blocks, use a lookup.

functions.name: isIp
functions.summary: The text is an address, v4 or v6. Text that is not one is `false`. Null stays null.

examples.note: the same call, written as a function

functions.name: ipNormalize
functions.summary: The address in one spelling. Leading zeros go. IPv6 is lowercase and its longest run of zero groups is compressed. Two spellings of one address come out the same.

examples.note: a dotted quad takes no leading zero

functions.name: ipScope
functions.summary: Where the address reaches: `unspecified`, `loopback`, `link-local`, `multicast`, `private` or `public`. Private is RFC 1918 and `fc00::/7`.

functions.name: inCidr
functions.summary: The address is in one of the blocks. A block of the other family holds nothing. A bare address is a block of one.

examples.note: any number of blocks
the other family
a bare address is a block of one
a block that does not parse

functions.name: cidrNetwork
functions.summary: The address masked to `prefix` bits, written as a block. Group by it to count per subnet.

examples.note: past the width of the address

functions.name: communityId
functions.signature: communityId(srcIp, srcPort, dstIp, dstPort, transport, seed)
functions.summary: The flow's [Community ID](https://github.com/corelight/community-id-spec), version 1. `transport` is an IANA protocol number, 0 to 255, as a number or as text, or one of these names in any case: `icmp`, `igmp`, `tcp`, `udp`, `gre`, `icmpv6` (or `ipv6-icmp`), `eigrp`, `ospf`, `pim`, `sctp`. Any other name is null. TCP, UDP and SCTP need both ports, 1 to 65535; for ICMP and ICMPv6 the ports are the type and the code; any other protocol has no ports. Both addresses must be IPv4 or both IPv6. `seed` is optional, 0 to 65535, 0 by default. Both directions of a flow give one ID.

examples.note: the reply, with the protocol's number
a seed
TCP needs both ports
not a protocol name it knows

groups.title: URLs, domains and user agents
groups.blurb: Text that does not read is null and throws a `CoercionRefused` exception on the record; blank text is null and throws nothing.

functions.name: urlDecode
functions.summary: `%XX` as the byte it names and `+` as a space, as a form field is encoded, and the bytes read as UTF-8; a byte that is not UTF-8 becomes U+FFFD. A `%` that two hex digits do not follow stays a `%`, so every text reads.

examples.note: a bare % stays

functions.name: htmlStrip
functions.summary: The text without its markup. A tag goes, in any case. A block-level tag, start or end, becomes a line break: `address`, `article`, `aside`, `blockquote`, `br`, `dd`, `div`, `dl`, `dt`, `fieldset`, `figcaption`, `figure`, `footer`, `form`, `h1` to `h6`, `header`, `hgroup`, `hr`, `li`, `nav`, `noscript`, `ol`, `output`, `p`, `pre`, `section`, `table`, `tbody`, `td`, `tfoot`, `th`, `thead`, `tr` and `ul`. A comment, a `<!...>` or `<?...>` declaration, and a `<script>` or `<style>` element go with what they hold; a `<![CDATA[...]]>` section leaves what it holds. A character reference becomes its character: a number, `é` or `é`, or any of HTML 4's names, such as `&`, ` ` or `ö`. A reference that does not read, and a `<` that starts no tag, stay as they are. Text without both `<` and `>` is returned as it is.

examples.note: named and numeric references
a block-level tag breaks the line

functions.name: parseUrl
functions.summary: A URL's parts as an object: `domain`, `fragment`, `path`, `extension`, `port`, `query`, `scheme`, `user_info`, `username` and `password`. Text that reads as an RFC 3986 URI or relative reference, such as a bare path, has its path, query, fragment and user info decoded. An `http`, `https`, `ftp`, `file` or `jar` URL that does not, holding a space or a `|` say, is split as written, undecoded. `extension` is what follows the last `.` of the path's last segment. `username` is the user info up to its first `:`, all of it where there is none, and `password` what follows that `:`. A part the URL lacks is null.

examples.note: a part read on its own
a path alone

functions.name: registeredDomain
functions.summary: The host, the name registered under its public suffix, that suffix and what is left, as an object of `domain`, `registered_domain`, `top_level_domain` and `subdomain`. The suffixes are the ICANN section of the Public Suffix List, compiled in. A host with no known suffix does not read.

examples.note: a suffix alone
no known suffix

functions.name: parseUserAgent
functions.summary: The browser, operating system and device a User-Agent header names, as an object of `name`, `version`, `os.name`, `os.version`, `os.full` and `device.name`. The rules are uap-core's, compiled in. `name` and `device.name` are `Other` where no rule matches, and `os` is null where none names an operating system. `os.full` is `os.name`, then `os.version` where there is one.

examples.expr: "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.6099.109 Safari/537.36".parseUserAgent()

examples.note: one part

exceptions.when: A parser got nothing from the record: malformed JSON, an unterminated CSV quote, a Grok pattern that matched nothing.
One declared field could not be read as its declared type while the rest of the record parsed. That field is null.
Two keys of a record contradict after flattening, such as the same key twice. One is kept.
A value could not convert to the type asked for, as in `parseInt("many")`. The result is null.
`i64` arithmetic overflowed. The result is null.
A division by zero. The result is null, not Infinity.
A parse met `NaN`, `Infinity` or a number past `f64`'s range. That key has no value.
A `while` loop hit its time budget with the record's condition still true.
An array read or write, or a string read, named a position the value does not have. The read is null and the write does nothing.
Bytes that did not decode under the source's encoding were replaced with U+FFFD.
A source set to `auto` recognized neither UTF-8 nor UTF-16 and guessed the encoding. The text may well be right.
No route or delivery condition took it.
No pipeline could finish the record: one crashed on its batch, or the record does not fit the memory budget alone.

recordFields.name: _raw
recordFields.what: The text the source received, decoded with the source's `encoding`. A parser reads it. The destination delivers it with the record unless a step sets it to `null`. A source whose `encoding` is `none` gives no `_raw`.

recordFields.name: __source.name
recordFields.what: The name of the source that read the record.

recordFields.name: __source.type
recordFields.what: The kind of source that read it, its `type`, such as `kafka`, `s3List`, `httpApi` or `hecReceiver`.

recordFields.name: __source.topic
recordFields.what: The Kafka topic, or event hub, the record came from. A metrics record carries `__smeltr_metrics` and a logs record `__smeltr_logs`.

recordFields.name: __source.partition
recordFields.what: The Kafka or Event Hubs partition the record came from.

recordFields.name: __source.offset
recordFields.what: The record's offset in its Kafka or Event Hubs partition, or its record number in its object, from 0.

recordFields.name: __source.bucket
recordFields.what: The bucket, or Azure container, the record's object is in.

recordFields.name: __source.key
recordFields.what: The key, or Azure blob name, of the object the record was read from.

recordFields.name: __source.url
recordFields.what: The address of the page an API source read the record from.

recordFields.name: __source.database
recordFields.what: The database an SQL source read the record from, as `host:port/database`.

recordFields.name: __source.remote
recordFields.what: The address of the sender that delivered the record to a receiver.

recordFields.name: __source.host
recordFields.what: The host a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none.

recordFields.name: __source.source
recordFields.what: The source a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none.

recordFields.name: __source.sourcetype
recordFields.what: The sourcetype a HEC sender filed the event under, or null where it named none.

recordFields.name: __source.index
recordFields.what: The index a HEC sender filed the event under, or an Elasticsearch client's bulk action named for its document; null where it named none.

recordFields.name: __source.id
recordFields.what: The `_id` an Elasticsearch client's bulk action named for its document, or null where it named none.

recordFields.name: __source.pipeline
recordFields.what: The ingest pipeline an Elasticsearch client's bulk action, or its request's `pipeline` query, named for its document, or null where neither named one.

recordFields.name: __source.time
recordFields.what: The time a sender gave the event, null otherwise.

recordFields.name: __source.fields
recordFields.what: The indexed fields a HEC sender gave the event, or null where it gave none. Read one as text with `__source.fields.env as str`.

recordFields.name: __source.resource
recordFields.what: The resource an OTLP log record came under: its attributes, each keeping its own type, or null where the export named none. Read one as text with `__source.resource["service.name"] as str`.

recordFields.name: __source.scope.name
recordFields.what: The name of the instrumentation scope an OTLP log record came under, the library that wrote it, or null where the export named none.

recordFields.name: __source.scope.version
recordFields.what: The version of that instrumentation scope, or null where the export named none.

recordFields.name: __source.scope.attributes
recordFields.what: That instrumentation scope's attributes, each keeping its own type, or null where the export named none.

recordFields.name: __source.headers
recordFields.what: The Kafka record's headers, each key to its value as text. A key the record repeats holds its last value, and a header with no value is not there. Read one as text with `__source.headers.trace as str`.

recordFields.name: __source.bytes
recordFields.what: The record's payload as the source read it, before any decoding. The source decodes `_raw` from it. A `bytes` destination writes it unless the destination names another field. Text functions refuse it; `decode(__source.bytes, encoding)` reads it as text.

recordFields.name: __destination.topic
recordFields.what: The Kafka topic or Event Hub a destination writes the record to. Null means the default value for that destination.

recordFields.name: __destination.index
recordFields.what: The index an Elasticsearch or Splunk HEC destination files the record under. Null means the destination's default index. A Splunk HEC destination on the `raw` endpoint refuses a record naming an index other than its own.

recordFields.name: __destination.prefix
recordFields.what: What an S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob Storage destination's object key starts with, taken as it is. Null means the destination's own prefix, with its time placeholders filled in.

recordFields.name: __destination.id
recordFields.what: The Elasticsearch document ID, used when the destination's document ID setting is `dedupe` or `overwrite`. When it is null, the destination's id field names the field that gives it, and with neither the document is sent with no ID.

recordFields.name: smeltr.exception
recordFields.what: The exceptions of a record answered tag or deliver: `route`, `pipeline`, and `exceptions`, a list of each one's `step`, `kind` and `message`.

types.name: i64
types.holds: A 64-bit signed integer. A result that does not fit is null, with an `Overflow` exception.

types.name: f64
types.holds: A 64-bit floating-point number. `/` on two numbers always gives one.

types.name: str
types.holds: Text, always valid UTF-8. Positions and lengths count characters.

types.name: bytes
types.holds: Bytes, not read as text. Text functions refuse them; `decode` reads them as text in a named encoding. They write as base64, and `toString` names another form.

types.name: datetime
types.holds: An instant in UTC, to the microsecond, written as ISO 8601.

types.name: duration
types.holds: A signed span, to the microsecond, written as its count of microseconds.

types.name: variant
types.holds: A value whose type is known only per row, such as a field of an open object that no declaration names.

types.name: array<T>
types.holds: Elements of one type, as many as each row has.

types.name: {name: T, ...}
types.holds: Named fields. `{ip: str}` holds only the fields it names; `{ip: str, ...}` also keeps the others. See [Objects](#objects).

examples.note: a negated test is true when the field is null

rejected.why: Text and a number have no common type. Convert first: `"10".parseInt() * 2`.
